title: Program Development Life Cycle
overview: A program development life cycle is the planned route a piece of software takes from an idea to a working, maintained product. Paper 2 asks why such a life cycle is used, why one model does not suit every project, and for the principles, benefits and drawbacks of the waterfall, iterative and rapid application development (RAD) models. It also asks what happens in the analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance stages. Answers score when each stage is described by what it produces (for example a requirements specification from analysis), when a model's benefit or drawback is tied to how that model works rather than listed from memory, and when a recommended model is justified against the details of the scenario given: how stable the requirements are, the size of the project, how available the client is and how quickly the software is needed.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of the purpose of a development life cycle.
Show understanding of the need for different development life cycles depending on the program being developed.
Describe the principles, benefits and drawbacks of each type of life cycle, including waterfall, iterative and rapid application development (RAD).
Show understanding of the analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance stages in the program development life cycle.

definitions.definition: The ordered set of stages that software passes through during its development and use: analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance. When maintenance can no longer keep the program fit for purpose, a new cycle begins.
The document produced by analysis that states precisely what the new system must do and any constraints on it; later stages design, build and test against it.
A linear life cycle in which each stage is finished and signed off before the next begins, with the output of one stage becoming the input to the next.

A life cycle that begins by building a small part of the requirements and then repeats cycles of planning, building, testing and review, each adding to a working version, until the whole system is complete.

A life cycle with minimal up-front planning in which modules are built as prototypes, often in parallel, refined through short cycles with frequent user feedback, and joined together for fast delivery.
A working model of part of a system, built quickly so that users can try it and say what should change.

Changes made to a program after it is in use: corrective (fixing faults found later), adaptive (responding to a new environment or new requirements) and perfective (improving performance or usability).

sections.title: The purpose of a development life cycle
content: A small program for your own use can be written by thinking for a few minutes and then typing. Commercial software is different: it is larger, involves a team, and is paid for by a client who expects particular results. A development life cycle gives that work a defined structure. The job is divided into stages (analysis, design, coding, testing and maintenance), each with a clear purpose and a clear output, so that progress can be planned, checked and managed.

Working to a life cycle means the problem is understood before anything is built, the solution is planned before it is coded, and the product is tested against what the client actually asked for. It also makes it easier to estimate time and cost, to share the work between team members, and to produce documentation along the way. The stages form a cycle because, when a program can no longer be maintained to meet its users' needs, the process starts again with a fresh analysis.
bullets: Purpose: give development a structured, manageable sequence of stages with defined outputs.
Benefits: the problem is understood first, work can be planned and costed, progress can be measured, the product is checked against the requirements.
Stages: analysis → design → coding → testing → maintenance, and back to analysis when the system is no longer fit for purpose.

sections.title: Analysis
content: Analysis is about understanding the problem, not solving it yet. The analyst investigates the current system if there is one, for example by interviewing users, observing how they work and examining existing documents, and uses abstraction to concentrate on what matters. The problem is then defined clearly and precisely: the inputs, the outputs, the processing needed between them and any constraints, such as hardware, budget, deadlines or rules on the data.

The result is a requirements specification that the client can agree to. Possible solutions may be compared at this stage and the most suitable one chosen. Everything later is judged against this document, so a requirement missed here tends to surface much later, when it is expensive to fix.
bullets: Investigate the problem and any existing system (interviews, observation, documents).
Define inputs, outputs, processing and constraints precisely.
Output: an agreed requirements specification; possible solutions compared and one chosen.
A requirement missed in analysis usually shows up only in testing or after release.

examples.label: Worked example: a testing fault traced back to analysis
examples.content:
A program works out a student's grade from three test scores. The requirements said "average three scores" and never considered a student who was absent for one test.

Testing: a tester enters 0 for the missed test. The average falls from 70 (marks 68 and 72) to 46.7, and the grade drops sharply.

Where is the fault?
   Coding? No. The code averages three numbers, exactly as designed.
   Design? No. The design follows the specification it was given.
   Analysis? Yes. "A score may be missing" was never identified as a requirement.

Fix: go back to analysis and add the requirement (e.g. average only the tests actually taken), then update the design, then the code, then re-test.
Patching the code alone (e.g. ignoring every 0) would wrongly discard a genuine mark of 0.

sections.title: Design
content: Design decides how the requirements will be met, in enough detail that a programmer could build the solution from it. A useful starting point is an identifier table listing the data the program needs. From that the designer chooses data structures (a 1D or 2D array, a record) and decides whether data must be kept permanently in a file. The program is decomposed into modules, shown on a structure chart, and each algorithm is planned as a flowchart or in pseudocode (see 12.2). Test data can also be planned here.
Design mistakes are much cheaper to correct on paper than after the code has been written, which is why it comes before coding.
bullets: Plan data: identifier table, data structures, files.
Plan structure: decomposition into modules on a structure chart.
Plan logic: flowcharts or pseudocode for each module; plan test data.

sections.title: Coding (implementation)
content: In coding, often called implementation, the design is turned into program code. A suitable high-level language has to be chosen, taking into account what the problem needs and what the team knows well. The pseudocode is then translated into that language, module by module.

Code rarely works first time. Syntax errors stop it compiling, and once it runs it may crash or give wrong output, so the programmer debugs as they go. Each module is normally tested on its own as it is written, and tested again after every change, so that fixing one thing does not break another.
bullets: Choose a suitable programming language; translate the design into code.
Remove syntax errors so it translates, then debug crashes and wrong output.
Test each module as it is written and again after each change.

sections.title: Testing
content: Getting some output is not the same as the program being correct. Testing checks, in a planned and thorough way, that the whole program meets every requirement in the specification, accepts valid input, rejects invalid input sensibly and behaves reliably in all situations. Normal, boundary and erroneous test data and methods such as white-box, black-box, alpha and beta testing are covered in 12.3.

When a test fails, the cause is traced back to the stage where it began, which may be coding, design or even analysis. Testing can show that errors are present but can never prove that none are left, which is one reason maintenance is needed later.
bullets: Check the whole program against the requirements specification.
Use planned test data covering valid, boundary and invalid input (details in 12.3).
A failed test is traced back to the stage that caused it; testing cannot prove a program is error-free.

sections.title: Maintenance
content: Once the software is in use, maintenance keeps it useful. Corrective maintenance fixes faults that testing missed. Adaptive maintenance changes the program because its environment or the requirements have changed, for example new hardware, a new operating system or a new law. Perfective maintenance makes the program better without changing what it does, such as making it faster or easier to use. The three types are covered fully in 12.3.

Maintenance can carry on for years, and it relies on the documentation produced in earlier stages. When changes can no longer keep the system fit for purpose, a new analysis begins, which is what makes the process a cycle rather than a straight line.
bullets: Corrective: fix faults found after release.
Adaptive: respond to a changed environment or changed requirements.
Perfective: improve performance or usability.
When maintenance is no longer enough, the cycle restarts with analysis.

sections.title: The waterfall model
content: Principles: the stages are carried out one after another, like water falling down steps. Each stage is completed, and its output (the specification, the design, the code) is passed down as the input to the next. All requirements are fixed at the start. Arrows back up to the previous stage allow for going back when more work is found to be needed, but the model assumes this is rare. Nothing usable is delivered until the end.

Benefits: it is simple to understand and easy to manage, because every stage has a defined output and a clear end point; one stage is handled at a time; and it suits smaller projects whose requirements are well understood and fixed. Drawbacks: working software appears only late in the project; changing requirements cannot easily be accommodated; progress inside a stage is hard to measure; modules are brought together only at the end, so integration problems are found late; and it is a poor choice for complex, long-running or ongoing projects.
bullets: Principle: strictly sequential stages, each finished before the next; requirements fixed at the start.
Benefits: simple, easy to manage, clear milestones and outputs; good for small, well-understood projects.
Drawbacks: no working product until late, cannot cope with changing requirements, late integration, poor for large or long projects.

sections.title: The iterative model
content: Principles: development does not wait for a complete specification. A small subset of the requirements is built first, giving a working, if limited, version. It is then reviewed, more requirements are identified, and another cycle of design, coding and testing adds to it. The cycles repeat until the whole system is complete, often tackling the highest-risk parts first.

Benefits: a working model exists early, so design or functional flaws are spotted and corrected quickly; the client can try each version and give feedback; progress is visible after each cycle; changing the scope costs less; each increment is small, so it is easier to test and debug; and lessons from one cycle improve the next. It suits large and mission-critical projects. Drawbacks: it needs more resources and management; a small system may be hard to split into useful increments; because not all requirements are known at the start, the overall design may need reworking later; and planning the increments may require a view of the complete system anyway.
bullets: Principle: build a small part, review, then add more in repeated cycles until complete.
Benefits: early working versions, early fault detection, regular client feedback, measurable progress, lower cost of change, risks tackled early.
Drawbacks: more resources, hard to divide small systems, design issues from requirements that arrive late.

sections.title: Rapid application development (RAD)
content: Principles: RAD replaces detailed up-front planning with prototyping. Modules are built as prototypes, often by separate small teams at the same time, and users try them and suggest changes. Analysis, design, coding and testing are squeezed into a series of short, repeated cycles, requirements are allowed to change as the work proceeds, and the finished prototypes are joined together to give the complete product quickly.

Benefits: much shorter development time; changing requirements are welcomed rather than resisted; users give feedback from the first review, so the product matches what they need; integrating from the start avoids a big integration problem at the end; progress is measurable; and components are often reused. Drawbacks: the system must be one that can be split into modules; it needs highly skilled developers and designers; users must be available and involved throughout; and it is best suited to component-based projects that need a short development time. Speed can also mean less formal documentation.
bullets: Principle: minimal planning, prototypes built in parallel, short feedback cycles, prototypes integrated into the final product.
Benefits: fast delivery, flexible requirements, strong user feedback, early integration, component reuse.
Drawbacks: needs modular systems, skilled staff and constant user involvement; documentation may be thin.

sections.title: Why different programs need different life cycles
content: No single model suits every program. The right choice depends on how clearly the requirements are known and whether they will change, the size and complexity of the system, how much risk is involved, how quickly something usable is needed, how skilled the team is, and whether the client can take part throughout.

Waterfall fits a small or well-understood job with fixed, agreed requirements, such as software that must follow a fixed standard. The iterative model fits a large or critical system where the full requirements emerge over time and early working versions reduce risk. RAD fits a system that has to be delivered quickly, can be split into components and has users available to test prototypes, such as a business app whose screens need regular user input.
bullets: Deciding factors: stability of requirements, size and complexity, risk, deadline, team skill, client availability.
Fixed, clear requirements and a small project → waterfall.
Large or critical project with evolving requirements → iterative.
Short deadline, modular system, users available throughout → RAD.

examples.label: Worked example: matching scenarios to life cycles
examples.content:
Scenario A: a program to calculate payroll deductions to a tax rule that is fully published and will not change this year. Small team, fixed deadline.
   → Waterfall. Requirements are complete and stable, so each stage can be finished and signed off in order; the clear milestones make it easy to manage.

Scenario B: a hospital system for patient records, scheduling and prescriptions, to be used for many years; staff are not yet sure of every feature they need.
   → Iterative. Build the high-risk records core first, deliver working versions, and add features as requirements become clear; each increment is tested on its own.

Scenario C: a shop needs a customer ordering app in eight weeks. The manager can meet the developers every week to try screens.
   → RAD. Tight deadline, the app splits into separate screens/modules built in parallel as prototypes, and the available user gives constant feedback.

diagram.title: The program development life cycle
nodes: Analysis: investigate the problem, agree the requirements specification
Design: data structures, structure chart, algorithms, test plan
Coding: translate the design into a programming language, debug modules
Testing: check the whole program against the requirements
Maintenance: corrective, adaptive and perfective changes in use; when no longer fit for purpose, return to analysis

analysisChains.title: Why waterfall struggles when requirements change
steps: In waterfall, requirements are fixed at analysis and each later stage builds on the previous stage's output
The client sees working software only near the end of the project
If the client then realises a key feature is wrong or missing, the change affects the specification, the design and the code
Several completed stages must be reopened, adding cost and delay
analysisChains.evaluation: Waterfall works well only when requirements are clear and stable at the start; where they are likely to change, an iterative or RAD approach, which shows working versions early, finds such problems while they are still cheap to fix.

analysisChains.title: How the iterative model reduces risk on a large project
steps: The team identifies the riskiest part of the system and builds it in the first increment
The increment is tested and reviewed with the client, so faults and misunderstandings appear early
What is learned is carried into the planning of the next increment
Each cycle delivers a larger working product, so progress can be measured
analysisChains.evaluation: Tackling risk first and reviewing often means major problems are found when little depends on them. The cost is extra resources and the chance that a design based on early, incomplete requirements needs reworking.

analysisChains.title: When RAD is not a good choice
steps: RAD depends on users trying prototypes and giving feedback throughout
It also depends on the system being divisible into modules that small, skilled teams can build in parallel
Suppose the client can meet developers only at the start and end, and the system is one tightly linked calculation engine
Neither condition holds: prototypes would get no feedback, and the work cannot be split among parallel teams
analysisChains.evaluation: RAD's speed comes from constant user involvement and modular, parallel building. Without them it loses its advantages, and a more planned model such as waterfall (if requirements are clear) or iterative would be a better fit.

examTips: For 'describe the principles', say how the model runs (the order of stages, when requirements are fixed, how often software is delivered), not just its name or its benefits.
Tie each benefit or drawback to the principle behind it: waterfall delivers late because each stage must finish first; RAD needs users throughout because it relies on prototype feedback.
When recommending a model for a scenario, quote the scenario details (changing requirements, deadline, project size, client availability) in your justification.
Describe a stage by its activities and its output: analysis produces the requirements specification, design produces structure charts and pseudocode, and so on.
Remember the five stages named in the syllabus: analysis, design, coding, testing, maintenance.
commonMistakes: Describing waterfall as allowing no return to an earlier stage at all; the model does allow going back, but it is costly and assumed to be rare.
Confusing the iterative model with RAD: iterative adds planned increments to a working system, while RAD relies on quickly built prototypes and continuous user feedback with minimal planning.
Giving generic benefits such as 'it is faster' or 'it is better' without saying why the model's principles produce them.
Treating testing as the only place faults are fixed, rather than tracing a fault back to the stage (analysis, design or coding) where it began.
Listing RAD's need for skilled developers and user involvement as benefits instead of as conditions that can make it unsuitable.
Leaving out maintenance, or treating the life cycle as ending when the program is delivered.

quickRecall.question: What is the purpose of a program development life cycle?
quickRecall.answer: To give development a structured sequence of stages with defined outputs, so the work can be planned, managed and checked against the requirements.

quickRecall.question: Name the stages of the program development life cycle.
quickRecall.answer: Analysis, design, coding (implementation), testing and maintenance.

quickRecall.question: What is the main output of the analysis stage?
quickRecall.answer: A requirements specification defining what the system must do and any constraints.

quickRecall.question: State one benefit and one drawback of the waterfall model.
quickRecall.answer: Benefit: simple and easy to manage, with clear stages and outputs. Drawback: no working software until late, and changing requirements are hard to accommodate.

quickRecall.question: How does the iterative model begin?
quickRecall.answer: By building a small subset of the requirements, then adding to it through repeated cycles of review, design, coding and testing.

quickRecall.question: What is a prototype, and why does RAD use them?
quickRecall.answer: A working model of part of a system; RAD uses prototypes so users can give feedback quickly instead of relying on detailed up-front planning.

quickRecall.question: Give two conditions a project needs for RAD to be suitable.
quickRecall.answer: Any two of: the system can be split into modules; skilled developers are available; users can be involved throughout; a short development time is required.

quickRecall.question: Why is it called a life cycle?
quickRecall.answer: Because when maintenance can no longer keep the program fit for purpose, development begins again with a new analysis.
